hypotheses.title: CoinbaseSmartWallet executeWithoutChainIdValidation allows cross-chain replay of owner changes
hypotheses.description: The `executeWithoutChainIdValidation()` function intentionally omits chain ID from the userOpHash, allowing the same signed UserOperation to be replayed across all chains where the wallet has the same address. The whitelisted selectors include `addOwnerAddress`, `addOwnerPublicKey`, `removeOwnerAtIndex`, and `upgradeToAndCall`. An attacker who obtains a valid signature for one of these operations on one chain can replay it on any other chain where the wallet exists at the same address. While this is documented as intentional for syncing owner changes, the `upgradeToAndCall` selector is particularly dangerous: a signed upgrade on one chain can be replayed on another chain to upgrade to a malicious implementation, potentially draining funds on chains the signer never intended to modify.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Owner signs a UserOperation calling `upgradeToAndCall` on chain A. 2. Attacker observes the signed UserOperation (e.g., from mempool or by being the bundler). 3. Attacker replays the same UserOperation on chain B where the wallet has the same address. 4. The wallet on chain B upgrades to the implementation specified in the signed data. 5. If the implementation is malicious or chain-specific, funds on chain B are compromised.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of funds on chains where the operation was not intended to be executed. Owner changes and upgrades can be forced on unintended chains.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove `upgradeToAndCall` from `canSkipChainIdValidation()` whitelist, or require explicit chain-specific signatures for upgrades. Consider adding a chain ID commitment for sensitive operations.

hypotheses.title: MagicSpend nonce marked used before signature validation allows griefing
hypotheses.description: `withdraw()` calls `_validateRequest()` which sets `_nonceUsed[nonce][account] = true` before checking `isValidWithdrawSignature()`. Any caller can submit a `WithdrawRequest` with an arbitrary nonce for any `account` (msg.sender is the account), consuming that nonce permanently even though the signature check reverts. The legitimate owner's signed request with that nonce can then never be used.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker builds a UserOperation with `sender = victimAccount`, `paymasterAndData` encoding a `WithdrawRequest` with a nonce the victim plans to use and a garbage signature. 2. Attacker submits to EntryPoint; `validatePaymasterUserOp` runs, `_validateRequest` sets `_nonceUsed[nonce][victim] = true`, then signature check fails and validationData=1. 3. EntryPoint rejects the op, but the victim's nonce is now permanently consumed, so the victim's legitimate signed withdraw request with that nonce reverts with `InvalidNonce`.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent denial of service on the victim's withdraw requests for any nonce the attacker can guess or front-run; victim funds remain locked in MagicSpend until a new nonce is signed.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move the `_nonceUsed` write to after signature validation succeeds, or perform signature validation before marking the nonce used.

hypotheses.title: CoinbaseSmartWallet.initialize() callable by anyone on uninitialized proxy
hypotheses.description: `initialize()` has no access control and only checks `nextOwnerIndex() != 0`. The factory deploys the proxy via `LibClone.createDeterministicERC1967` and then calls `initialize(owners)`. Between proxy deployment and the factory's `initialize` call there is no window (same tx), but any proxy deployed directly (or via a front-run on a predicted address before the factory's `createAccount` executes) can be initialized by an attacker with attacker-controlled owners. Because the address is deterministic from `(owners, nonce)`, an attacker who knows the intended owners can pre-deploy the proxy at that address and call `initialize` with their own owners, then the factory's `createAccount` sees `alreadyDeployed == true` and skips initialization — leaving the account owned by the attacker.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Victim computes intended account address via `getAddress(owners, nonce)`. 2. Attacker front-runs by deploying the ERC1967 proxy at that exact address (using the same implementation and salt) and calls `initialize([attackerOwner])`. 3. Victim's `createAccount` call finds `alreadyDeployed == true` and skips `initialize`. 4. Attacker now controls the wallet that the victim believes is theirs.
hypotheses.impact: Complete takeover of the victim's smart wallet; loss of all funds sent to that address.
hypotheses.recommendation: Have the factory always call `initialize` and have `initialize` be idempotent-safe, or restrict `initialize` to be callable only by the factory (e.g., pass factory address and check `msg.sender`), or use an atomic deploy+initialize pattern that reverts if already initialized.

hypotheses.title: MagicSpend postOp assert can permanently lock withdrawable ETH
hypotheses.description: The `postOp` function uses `assert(mode != PostOpMode.postOpReverted)`, which on failure consumes all forwarded gas and reverts. If the user account's `receive()` reverts or OOGs during the `forceSafeTransferETH`, EntryPoint re-invokes `postOp` with `postOpReverted`, which hits the assert and reverts, causing the entire UserOperation to revert. Since `_withdrawableETH[account]` was already deleted before the transfer, the withdrawable funds cannot be recovered through `withdrawGasExcess` either, and the account's deposit on EntryPoint still pays for gas.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker controls an account with a `receive()` that reverts (or provides insufficient gas stipend) and gets a valid signed withdraw request from the paymaster owner (e.g., via a legitimate gas sponsorship flow). 2) Attacker submits a UserOperation whose `postOp` transfer triggers a revert/OOG in their receiver. 3) EntryPoint retries `postOp` with `PostOpMode.postOpReverted`, hitting the assert and reverting the entire op while gas is consumed. 4) Attacker repeats to grief paymaster accounting / burn withheld funds.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of user funds (gas paid, withdrawable ETH deleted without transfer); unrecoverable state where `_withdrawableETH` is zeroed but ETH never delivered.
hypotheses.recommendation: Replace the `assert` with a graceful path that refunds the account by restoring `_withdrawableETH[account] += withdrawable`, or use a pull-based withdrawal instead of `forceSafeTransferETH` so the paymaster is not dependent on receiver behavior.

hypotheses.title: MagicSpend postOp uses assert, bricking UserOps on insufficient balance
hypotheses.description: `postOp` uses `assert(mode != PostOpMode.postOpReverted)`. If the contract's ETH balance is insufficient at postOp time (e.g., owner withdrew funds, or another user drained via `withdraw()`), `forceSafeTransferETH` will fail and the EntryPoint will re-enter `postOp` with `postOpReverted`, triggering the assert and consuming all gas. The validation-time balance check only covers the moment of validation, not postOp.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a pending UserOp relying on MagicSpend. 2) Attacker front-runs by calling `withdraw()` with their own valid request to drain contract ETH. 3) Victim's UserOp executes, `postOp` cannot transfer, EntryPoint re-enters with `postOpReverted`, assert reverts and burns all gas.
hypotheses.impact: Victim UserOp fails and pays full gas; contract can be griefed into reverting postOp paths.
hypotheses.recommendation: Replace `assert` with a graceful revert or handle `postOpReverted` by skipping the transfer.

hypotheses.title: WebAuthn.verify does not validate authenticatorData length before indexing
hypotheses.description: `verify()` accesses `webAuthnAuth.authenticatorData[32]` without checking that `authenticatorData.length > 32`. If an attacker supplies a short `authenticatorData`, the index access will revert (Solidity bounds check) or, in older versions, read out of bounds. This causes a revert rather than a clean `false` return, which can be used to grief callers that expect a boolean. More importantly, the `challengeIndex` and `typeIndex` are attacker-controlled and used in `slice()` without bounds validation, which can cause reverts or, if `slice` is lenient, incorrect parsing.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker submits a signature with a malformed `WebAuthnAuth` struct (short `authenticatorData` or out-of-range `challengeIndex`/`typeIndex`). 2. `verify()` reverts instead of returning `false`. 3. Callers like `_validateSignature` in `CoinbaseSmartWallet` propagate the revert, causing `validateUserOp` to revert rather than return validation failure.
hypotheses.impact: DoS on signature validation; user operations fail unexpectedly; potential griefing of ERC-1271 calls.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add explicit length checks for `authenticatorData` (>= 37 bytes) and validate `challengeIndex`/`typeIndex` are within `clientDataJSON` bounds before slicing.

hypotheses.title: MagicSpend withdraw() does not reserve gas, allows draining contract
hypotheses.description: `withdraw()` calls `_withdraw(withdrawRequest.asset, msg.sender, withdrawRequest.amount)` directly, transferring the full requested amount to the caller. Unlike `validatePaymasterUserOp`, it does not reserve `maxCost` for gas, and it does not check `address(this).balance >= amount` before transferring. The comment says "reserve funds for gas, will credit user with difference in post op" but no reservation actually occurs. A user with a valid signed withdraw request can withdraw the full amount, and if the same signed request is also used as a paymaster request, the contract may be drained.
hypotheses.impact: Contract insolvency — the paymaster may not have enough ETH to cover gas costs for other users' userOps, causing their transactions to fail.
hypotheses.recommendation: Reserve `maxCost` (or a gas buffer) in `withdraw()` similar to `validatePaymasterUserOp`, or require the caller to be the account itself and route through the paymaster flow.

hypotheses.title: MagicSpend nonce consumed before signature verification enables griefing
hypotheses.description: `withdraw()` calls `_validateRequest(msg.sender, withdrawRequest)` before checking the signature, and `_validateRequest` marks `_nonceUsed[nonce][account] = true` unconditionally. Any untrusted caller can front-run or blindly call `withdraw()` with an arbitrary `nonce` for `msg.sender` (their own address), permanently consuming that nonce. Because `_nonceUsed` is keyed by `msg.sender`, an attacker can only burn the nonces of their own address — but the signed withdraw request from the paymaster owner is account-bound, so the attacker must equal the intended account.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) The paymaster owner signs a `WithdrawRequest` for account A with nonce N (off-chain, e.g. as part of a Magic Spend flow). 2) Before account A's legitimate withdrawal tx lands, anyone observing the signature (or the mempool) can... actually the caller must be A. However, if A submits a `UserOperation`, EntryPoint calls `validatePaymasterUserOp` which invokes `_validateRequest` on `userOp.sender`, burning the nonce; then a later direct `withdraw()` by A on the same request reverts with InvalidNonce even though the UserOp may fail elsewhere. In addition, when `validatePaymasterUserOp` reverts after `_validateRequest` (e.g., due to `InsufficientBalance`), the nonce stays consumed because state writes are reverted with the whole tx only if that outer tx reverts; if it's later reverted within the UserOp, nonce is rolled back, but the ordering still allows any failure after `_validateRequest` in `withdraw` (e.g., signature OK, expiry pass) to consume the nonce prior to transfer failure.
hypotheses.impact: Legitimate signed withdraw requests become unusable; user funds locked in paymaster cannot be withdrawn via their pre-signed request.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move `_nonceUsed` marking to after all validations (signature and expiry) succeed, or at least require signature validation before consuming the nonce.

hypotheses.title: MagicSpend validatePaymasterUserOp consumes nonce before signature validation
hypotheses.description: In `validatePaymasterUserOp()`, `_validateRequest()` is called which marks the nonce as used, and then `isValidWithdrawSignature()` is checked. If the signature is invalid, `sigFailed` is set to 1 and validationData is returned with failure flag, but the nonce remains consumed. This means a UserOperation with an invalid signature will consume the nonce, preventing the legitimate user from using that nonce later. An attacker who can front-run or observe a UserOperation with a valid signature but cause it to fail (e.g., by manipulating gas or other parameters) could burn the nonce. More critically, if an attacker submits a UserOperation with a valid signature but the EntryPoint rejects it for other reasons after validation, the nonce is consumed.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker observes a legitimate UserOperation with a valid MagicSpend signature. 2. Attacker submits the same UserOperation but with a modification that causes the EntryPoint to reject it after `validatePaymasterUserOp` succeeds (e.g., by causing the account's `validateUserOp` to fail). 3. The nonce is consumed in `_validateRequest`. 4. The legitimate user's subsequent attempt to use the same nonce fails with `InvalidNonce`.
hypotheses.impact: Denial of service — legitimate withdraw requests cannot be executed because their nonces are consumed by failed attempts.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move the nonce consumption to after signature validation succeeds, or only consume the nonce when the signature is valid.

hypotheses.title: MultiOwnable removeOwnerAtIndex allows removing owner at index 0, bricking account
hypotheses.description: `removeOwnerAtIndex` allows removing any owner, including the last remaining owner. If all owners are removed, no one can call `onlyOwner` functions, and `_checkOwner` will always revert (unless called by the contract itself). The account becomes permanently bricked — no owner can add a new owner, upgrade, or execute.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A single owner (or a compromised owner key) calls `removeOwnerAtIndex(0)` to remove themselves. 2) If they are the only owner, the account has no owners. 3) All `onlyOwner` functions revert; the account is unusable.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent loss of account control and any funds held by the account.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require that at least one owner remains after removal, or provide a recovery mechanism.

hypotheses.title: MagicSpend postOp double-counts maxGasCost refund on postOpReverted
hypotheses.description: In `validatePaymasterUserOp`, `_withdrawableETH[userOp.sender] += withdrawAmount - maxCost` credits the user with the amount minus the max gas cost. In `postOp`, `withdrawable = _withdrawableETH[account] + (maxGasCost - actualGasCost)` adds back the unused gas. If `actualGasCost > maxGasCost` (possible when the EntryPoint charges more than the maxCost passed at validation, e.g. due to postOp gas overhead), the subtraction underflows and reverts, but more importantly the accounting assumes `actualGasCost <= maxGasCost`. The `assert(mode != PostOpMode.postOpReverted)` also means a revert in postOp (e.g. from the transfer) will revert the whole userOp, but the `_withdrawableETH` was already deleted before the transfer, so funds are lost to the user.
hypotheses.impact: User loses the withdrawable balance if the ETH transfer in postOp fails (e.g. recipient contract reverts on receive), because `delete _withdrawableETH[account]` happens before the transfer and the assert prevents retry.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move `delete _withdrawableETH[account]` after the successful transfer, or use a pull-based pattern.

hypotheses.title: MagicSpend withdraw() does not check contract balance before transfer
hypotheses.description: `withdraw()` calls `_withdraw` which uses `SafeTransferLib.safeTransferETH`. Unlike `validatePaymasterUserOp`, there is no check that `address(this).balance >= withdrawRequest.amount`. If the contract's balance is insufficient (e.g., because funds were already credited to other users via `_withdrawableETH`), the transfer reverts, but the nonce was already consumed by `_validateRequest`, permanently burning the signed request.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a signed WithdrawRequest. 2) Attacker front-runs by draining the contract balance via another legitimate withdraw or by triggering paymaster ops that credit `_withdrawableETH`. 3) The victim's `withdraw()` reverts on transfer, but the nonce is already marked used, so the signed request is permanently unusable.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent loss of a signed withdraw authorization (funds effectively frozen for that request).
hypotheses.recommendation: Check `address(this).balance >= withdrawRequest.amount` before consuming the nonce, or move nonce consumption after the transfer succeeds.

hypotheses.title: MagicSpend postOp asserts mode != postOpReverted causing DoS on revert
hypotheses.description: `postOp()` uses `assert(mode != PostOpMode.postOpReverted)`. The EntryPoint calls `postOp` with `postOpReverted` mode when the user operation's inner call reverts after the paymaster was charged. The comment claims this is "impossible" because balance is checked at validation, but the user's `receive()`/fallback can revert (e.g., a contract account that rejects ETH), or the account can consume gas such that the transfer fails. An `assert` consumes all gas and reverts, which the EntryPoint treats as a paymaster failure.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker (as the account owner) crafts a UserOp whose execution causes the account to reject the ETH transfer in `postOp` (e.g., a `receive()` that reverts, or a call that drains gas). 2. EntryPoint calls `postOp` with `postOpReverted` mode. 3. `assert` fails, reverting the whole `postOp`, which the EntryPoint interprets as a paymaster violation and may penalize/ban the paymaster.
hypotheses.impact: Paymaster can be throttled/banned by the EntryPoint, and the user's withdrawable funds accounting (`_withdrawableETH`) is not cleared, potentially leaving stale state.
hypotheses.recommendation: Replace `assert` with a graceful handling path (e.g., return early or revert with a custom error) that does not consume all gas and does not leave inconsistent state.

hypotheses.title: withdrawGasExcess reverts on zero causing unrecoverable zero-value cleanup
hypotheses.description: `withdrawGasExcess` reverts with `NoExcess()` when `_withdrawableETH[msg.sender] == 0`. While not directly a fund loss, any integrator that calls this as a no-op cleanup path will revert, blocking composite flows that intend to drain excess as part of a larger batch. This converts an intended idempotent cleanup into a hard revert.
hypotheses.attackPath: Caller relies on `withdrawGasExcess()` returning silently when zero; a malicious contract calls it in a batch to force a revert on the caller's tx.
hypotheses.impact: Failed flows / griefing on integrating calls; no direct fund loss.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove the revert and return silently on zero, or document the requirement for callers to pre-check the balance.

hypotheses.title: Owner removal does not recompact indices, leaving ownerIndex validation gaps
hypotheses.description: `removeOwnerAtIndex` deletes the owner at an index but does not decrement `nextOwnerIndex` or reuse indices. When the last owner is removed, an account can be left with no valid owners while `executeWithoutChainIdValidation`-replayable operations that were previously signed (e.g., for adding owners) can no longer be validated because `ownerAtIndex` returns empty and `_validateSignature` reverts. The account becomes unreachable for owner-driven recovery, especially if only WebAuthn owners existed and their credential is lost.
hypotheses.attackPath: A compromised owner calls `removeOwnerAtIndex` for every other owner. Even if legitimate, the account can be drained. From an untrusted-actor perspective, if the account permits replayable cross-chain owner removal with a stolen signature, anyone replaying that signature on other chains can also remove owners, leaving the account frozen.
hypotheses.impact: Account permanently locked; owners cannot be re-added through normal signature validation, funds stuck.
hypotheses.recommendation: Prevent removing the last owner, or ensure any index gaps still allow existing owners to be discovered (e.g., maintain an owner count and require >0 owners post-removal).

hypotheses.title: WebAuthn verify partially slices clientDataJSON enabling OOB revert
hypotheses.description: `verify()` calls `webAuthnAuth.clientDataJSON.slice(webAuthnAuth.typeIndex, webAuthnAuth.typeIndex + 21)` and `slice(challengeIndex, challengeIndex + expectedChallenge.length)` without bounding the indices to the string's length. A crafted `WebAuthnAuth` with out-of-range indices causes LibString.slice to revert, and only enables griefing if an attacker can inject arbitrary signature data — which they can because `_validateSignature` in CoinbaseSmartWallet decodes attacker-supplied bytes as `WebAuthnAuth` when `ownerBytes.length == 64`. That means a caller (via EntryPoint or via ERC-1271) can force a revert rather than returning `1`, potentially blocking legitimate `validateUserOp` simulation flows and reverting the whole UserOp instead of the intended "signature failed → return 1" path.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker submits a UserOperation with `userOp.signature` = abi.encode(SignatureWrapper{ownerIndex: validPasskeyOwnerIndex, signatureData: abi.encode(WebAuthnAuth with typeIndex = type(uint256).max ...)}). 2) `_validateSignature` decodes and calls WebAuthn.verify which reverts via slice. 3) Entire validateUserOp reverts, bypassing the intended return-1 semantics and potentially letting an attacker cause gas-heavy reverts against the paymaster.
hypotheses.impact: Griefing / blocking of the account's UserOps; validates revert instead of signature-failure return; potential gas griefing against paymasters.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bound-check the indices in `verify` and return false instead of reverting when out of range; or wrap _validateSignature calls so decoding/slice failures return false.

hypotheses.title: MultiOwnable._checkOwner allows address(this) as owner, enabling self-call privilege escalation
hypotheses.description: `_checkOwner()` returns success if `msg.sender == address(this)`. Combined with `execute()` and `executeBatch()` which are callable by the EntryPoint or an owner, this means any owner can craft a call that makes the wallet call itself, bypassing the `onlyOwner` check for functions like `addOwnerAddress`. This is by design (self-call is a legitimate owner action), but it means the `onlyEntryPointOrOwner` modifier on `execute` effectively grants owner privileges to any code path that can make the wallet call itself — including a malicious target contract that re-enters via a callback.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Owner calls `execute(maliciousTarget, 0, data)`. 2. `maliciousTarget` calls back into the wallet's `addOwnerAddress` (or any `onlyOwner` function). 3. `msg.sender == address(this)` is true, so `_checkOwner` passes. 4. Attacker-controlled owner is added.
hypotheses.impact: If an owner is tricked into calling a malicious contract, that contract can escalate to add/remove owners or upgrade the implementation.
hypotheses.recommendation: This is inherent to the self-call pattern; consider documenting the risk or restricting self-calls to specific selectors.

hypotheses.title: MagicSpend validatePaymasterUserOp allows withdrawAmount == maxCost leaving zero withdrawable
hypotheses.description: The check `if (withdrawAmount < maxCost) revert` allows `withdrawAmount == maxCost`. In that case `_withdrawableETH[userOp.sender] += 0`, and in `postOp` the user receives `maxGasCost - actualGasCost` (the unused gas). This is fine, but if `actualGasCost == maxGasCost`, the user receives nothing and the entire withdrawAmount is consumed by gas. This is expected behavior but the user may not realize their full withdraw request is consumed by gas.
hypotheses.impact: User's withdraw request is fully consumed by gas with no funds returned; potential user confusion but not a protocol loss.
hypotheses.recommendation: Document clearly or require `withdrawAmount > maxCost` with a minimum buffer.

hypotheses.title: CoinbaseSmartWallet executeWithoutChainIdValidation lacks bounds check on data
hypotheses.description: `bytes4 selector = bytes4(data[0:4]);` will revert if `data.length < 4`, but more importantly the function is called via `_call(address(this), 0, data)` which re-enters the wallet. The `canSkipChainIdValidation` whitelist includes `upgradeToAndCall`, `addOwnerAddress`, `addOwnerPublicKey`, and `removeOwnerAtIndex`. An attacker who obtains a valid signature for a cross-chain replayable userOp can execute these functions on any chain where the wallet exists at the same address, potentially adding an attacker-controlled owner.
hypotheses.impact: Cross-chain replay of owner management operations could allow an attacker to take over wallets on other chains if they can obtain a valid signature for one chain.
hypotheses.recommendation: This is by design for the replayable nonce key, but ensure the signature includes chain-specific context or restrict the whitelist.

hypotheses.title: MagicSpend validatePaymasterUserOp does not enforce expiry as revert
hypotheses.description: The expiry is only packed into `validationData` via `(uint256(withdrawRequest.expiry) << 160)`. EntryPoint v0.6 interprets the upper 48 bits as `validUntil`, but the value is not masked to 48 bits and the semantics depend on EntryPoint enforcement. If EntryPoint does not enforce (or if the value overflows the 48-bit field), an expired signed request can still be used to sponsor a UserOperation, draining the paymaster's ETH balance.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains an old signed WithdrawRequest (e.g., leaked or reused). 2) Attacker crafts a UserOperation with that request as paymasterAndData. 3) If EntryPoint does not enforce validUntil (or the packed value is malformed), the op executes and the paymaster funds the gas.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of paymaster ETH funds via expired authorizations.
hypotheses.recommendation: Explicitly revert in `validatePaymasterUserOp` when `block.timestamp > withdrawRequest.expiry`, and mask expiry to 48 bits before packing.

hypotheses.title: MagicSpend.withdrawGasExcess reentrancy via forceSafeTransferETH
hypotheses.description: `withdrawGasExcess()` deletes `_withdrawableETH[msg.sender]` before calling `_withdraw`, which is correct ordering. However, `_withdraw` uses `SafeTransferLib.safeTransferETH` which forwards all gas to the recipient. If the recipient is a contract with a malicious `receive()`, it can reenter `withdrawGasExcess()` — but since the balance was already deleted, the second call reverts with `NoExcess`. The real risk is reentering `withdraw()` with a valid signed request during the ETH transfer, which could double-spend if the same signed request is used. Since `_validateRequest` marks the nonce before transfer, this is mitigated. The remaining risk is reentering `postOp` — but `postOp` is only callable by EntryPoint.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker is a contract account that calls `withdrawGasExcess`. 2. During the ETH transfer, `receive()` reenters `withdraw()` with a pre-signed request. 3. Nonce is marked before transfer, so replay is blocked. 4. However, if the attacker has multiple valid signed requests, they can drain multiple amounts in one tx.
hypotheses.impact: Multiple withdrawals in a single transaction if attacker holds multiple signed requests; limited by signature availability.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a reentrancy guard to `withdraw` and `withdrawGasExcess`.

hypotheses.title: CoinbaseSmartWalletFactory.createAccount front-runnable to initialize with attacker owners
hypotheses.description: `createAccount` deploys a deterministic address based on `owners` and `nonce`. If a user pre-computes their wallet address and sends funds to it before deployment, an attacker can front-run the `createAccount` call with the same `owners` and `nonce` (which are public in the mempool) and deploy the wallet first. Since `initialize` is called by the factory, the attacker's call initializes the wallet with the same owners — so this is not directly exploitable for owner takeover. However, if the attacker uses a different `owners` array that hashes to the same salt (collision), or if the user intended different owners, the attacker can deploy with attacker-controlled owners. More critically, the attacker can deploy the wallet with the correct owners but then the user's subsequent `createAccount` call will see `alreadyDeployed == true` and skip initialization — which is fine. The real risk is if the user's intended owners are not yet known and the attacker deploys with their own owners first.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. User computes their wallet address off-chain and sends funds to it. 2. Attacker observes the pending `createAccount` transaction in the mempool. 3. Attacker front-runs with `createAccount` using the same `owners` and `nonce` — this deploys the wallet with the correct owners, so no takeover. 4. Alternatively, if the user's `owners` are not yet public, the attacker cannot guess them. The attack requires the attacker to know the exact `owners` and `nonce`.
hypotheses.impact: If the attacker can deploy with different owners (e.g., by using a different `nonce` that produces the same address — not possible due to salt), they could take over. In practice, the salt includes `owners`, so the attacker must use the same owners.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `msg.sender` in the salt or require the deployer to be the first owner to prevent front-running.

hypotheses.title: executeWithoutChainIdValidation reverts on short calldata
hypotheses.description: `executeWithoutChainIdValidation(bytes calldata data)` performs `bytes4(data[0:4])` without checking `data.length >= 4`. If calldata is shorter than 4 bytes, the slice reverts, blocking the entire UserOp. Combined with `validateUserOp`'s requirement that the outer selector match, an attacker cannot exploit this against a legitimate owner directly, but it does mean a malformed EntryPoint-driven call reverts and can grief batching flows that assume short data is handled.
hypotheses.attackPath: If a downstream contract (e.g., a batch executor) blindly forwards calldata to this method, a caller can supply data with length < 4 to force a revert in the middle of a multi-call sequence.
hypotheses.impact: Denial of service for batched flows; no direct fund loss.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `require(data.length >= 4)` with a clear custom error, or pad short calldata.

hypotheses.title: MagicSpend withdraw() lacks expiry check ordering, allowing replay after expiry via nonce reuse pattern
hypotheses.description: `withdraw()` calls `_validateRequest` (which marks the nonce used) before checking `block.timestamp > withdrawRequest.expiry`. If the request is expired, the function reverts but the nonce is already consumed — this is a griefing vector but not a fund loss. However, the reverse concern: `validatePaymasterUserOp` does not check expiry at all (only encodes it in validationData), so an expired request can still be used in a UserOp if the EntryPoint ignores the expiry bits.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a signed request that has expired. 2) Submits it via a UserOp; `validatePaymasterUserOp` does not revert on expiry, only sets validationData. 3) If the bundler/EntryPoint does not enforce expiry, the request is honored.
hypotheses.impact: Expired signed requests remain usable, defeating the expiry protection.
hypotheses.recommendation: Explicitly revert in `validatePaymasterUserOp` when `block.timestamp > withdrawRequest.expiry`.

hypotheses.title: CoinbaseSmartWalletFactory createAccount does not verify implementation is a contract
hypotheses.category: Integration / wrong assumptions about external contracts
hypotheses.description: `createAccount()` uses `LibClone.createDeterministicERC1967` with `implementation` set in the constructor. If `implementation` is not a contract (e.g., an EOA or a self-destructed contract), the clone will be created but `initialize()` will be called on an address with no code, which will succeed silently (calling a non-contract address with calldata returns success with empty returndata). The account would then be a proxy pointing to a non-contract implementation, and all calls would succeed as no-ops, potentially locking funds sent to it.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Factory is deployed with a valid implementation. 2. Implementation is self-destructed (if it has a selfdestruct path) or the address is somehow not a contract. 3.
